Avoid using alcohol or substances to cope — they worsen PTSD long-term
short_term: Trauma-focused therapy (EMDR or trauma-focused CBT) is the most effective treatment
Medication (SSRIs like sertraline) can reduce symptoms while therapy is in progress
Grounding techniques for flashbacks: name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear
long_term: Treatment takes time — recovery is possible and most people do recover with proper support
Social support is essential — isolation worsens PTSD
Mental health services: Butabika Hospital, NGOs including TPO Uganda, AVSI Foundation

see_doctor_if: Flashbacks or nightmares about a traumatic event for more than 1 month
Avoiding places, people, or situations that remind you of the trauma
Feeling cut off from your emotions or other people
Any thoughts of self-harm
ptsd.local_context: PTSD is very prevalent in Uganda due to the aftermath of armed conflict in the north, displacement, domestic violence, and sexual violence. TPO Uganda (Transcultural Psychosocial Organisation) provides trauma-focused counselling in many districts. Reporting trauma-related symptoms to a health worker is a sign of strength, not weakness.
home_remedies: Physical exercise significantly reduces PTSD symptom severity
Mindfulness and breathing techniques reduce acute anxiety and hypervigilance
Social support — spending time with safe, trusted people is therapeutic
Avoid alcohol and substances — they temporarily numb pain but worsen PTSD

bipolar_disorder.name: Bipolar Disorder
bipolar_disorder.description: A brain disorder causing extreme mood swings — from euphoric 'highs' (mania or hypomania) to devastating lows (depression). Episodes can last days to months. Affects 1-2% of people. Requires lifelong management but people with bipolar disorder live full, productive lives.
bipolar_disorder.body_mechanism: Involves dysregulation of circuits between the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus, with abnormalities in serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. During mania, these systems are overactive; during depression, underactive. Sleep disruption is both a trigger and symptom of episodes.

immediate: If experiencing severe mania (not sleeping, very erratic behaviour, psychosis) — go to hospital urgently
Do not make major decisions (financial, relationship, work) during manic episodes
short_term: Mood stabiliser medication (lithium, valproate, carbamazepine) is the cornerstone of treatment
Lithium requires regular blood tests to monitor levels
Regular daily routine is essential — consistent sleep and wake times
long_term: Medication must be taken lifelong — stopping is the most common trigger for relapse
Sleep regulation is the single most important lifestyle factor
Therapy (CBT, family-focused therapy) alongside medication
Identify and manage personal triggers (stress, sleep disruption, substance use)

see_doctor_if: Periods of feeling extraordinarily energetic, needing little sleep, and very elevated mood
Periods of making reckless decisions (spending, sex, business) that you wouldn't normally make
Alternating with periods of severe depression
Any family member with bipolar disorder — genetic risk is significant
bipolar_disorder.local_context: Bipolar disorder is often misdiagnosed as depression in Uganda (only the depressive episodes are recognised). Lithium and carbamazepine are available at regional hospitals. Many people with bipolar disorder are accused of being 'bewitched' during manic episodes. Butabika Hospital has expertise in bipolar disorder management.
home_remedies: Strict sleep schedule — going to bed and waking at exactly the same time every day is the most powerful lifestyle intervention
Mood charting — tracking daily mood helps identify patterns and early warning signs
Reduce alcohol and caffeine — both destabilise mood significantly

chronic_kidney_disease.name: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
chronic_kidney_disease.description: Progressive and permanent damage to the kidneys over months to years. The kidneys lose their ability to filter waste and excess fluid from the blood. A silent disease — by the time symptoms appear, significant damage has often already occurred. Diabetes and hypertension are the two leading causes in Uganda.
chronic_kidney_disease.body_mechanism: Chronically elevated blood glucose (diabetes) or blood pressure damages the small blood vessels in the kidney glomeruli (filters). Over years these filters become scarred and non-functional. As kidney function falls below 15% (kidney failure), waste products accumulate in blood (uraemia), fluid builds up (oedema, breathlessness), and the kidneys can no longer maintain electrolyte balance.

immediate: If you have diabetes or hypertension — get kidney function tests (creatinine, eGFR) annually
Sudden severe reduction in urine output is a medical emergency — go to hospital
short_term: Control blood pressure aggressively — target below 130/80 mmHg
Control blood glucose if diabetic — HbA1c below 7%
Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) — they accelerate kidney damage
Avoid dehydration
Treat urinary tract infections promptly
long_term: Specialist nephrology review — available at Mulago and regional hospitals
Dietary changes: reduce protein, salt, potassium, phosphate as kidneys fail
Dialysis or kidney transplant for end-stage disease
Medications: ACE inhibitors (enalapril/lisinopril) slow CKD progression in diabetics and hypertensives

see_doctor_if: Foamy or bloody urine
Swollen ankles or legs especially in morning
Reduced urine output
Known diabetes or hypertension — get annual kidney function check
Fatigue and anaemia in someone with known kidney problems
chronic_kidney_disease.local_context: CKD is increasingly common in Uganda due to the rising burden of diabetes and hypertension. Kidney function tests (creatinine and urea) are available at district hospitals. Dialysis is available at Mulago, Kiruddu, and some regional hospitals but is expensive and limited. Preventing CKD through controlling diabetes and hypertension is far more effective than treating it.
home_remedies: Drink adequate water — dehydration accelerates kidney damage
Reduce salt intake significantly — eases hypertension which damages kidneys
Avoid traditional herbal medicines — many are nephrotoxic (damage kidneys)
Avoid taking painkillers (NSAIDs) unless prescribed — they reduce kidney blood flow

glaucoma.name: Glaucoma
glaucoma.description: A group of eye conditions where increased pressure in the eye damages the optic nerve, causing progressive irreversible vision loss. The leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Called the 'silent thief of sight' because vision loss is gradual and painless — until severe.
glaucoma.body_mechanism: The eye produces fluid (aqueous humour) that normally drains out. In glaucoma, drainage is impaired, pressure builds, and damages the optic nerve. Peripheral vision is lost first (tunnel vision), then central vision as damage progresses. Once the optic nerve is damaged, that vision cannot be restored.

immediate: Sudden eye pain with redness, blurred vision, and halos around lights is ACUTE angle-closure glaucoma — medical emergency — go to hospital immediately
Annual eye pressure checks for those over 40, with diabetes, or with family history of glaucoma
short_term: Treatment: eye drops to reduce pressure (timolol, latanoprost, bimatoprost)
Eye drops must be used every day — even when vision feels fine
Laser treatment (trabeculoplasty) or surgery (trabeculectomy) may be needed
long_term: Glaucoma management is lifelong — stops progression but cannot restore lost vision
Regular eye pressure monitoring every 3-6 months
Avoid medications that raise eye pressure — some antihistamines and antidepressants

see_doctor_if: Any gradual loss of side vision
Sudden eye pain with blurred vision — emergency
Halos around lights at night
You are over 40 — get annual eye check
Family member with glaucoma — you have a significantly elevated risk
glaucoma.local_context: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in Uganda and Africa. African-descent people have a 6-8 times higher risk than European populations. Eye care is available at regional hospitals with ophthalmic units. The Lions Eye Institute at Nakasero Hospital, Kampala provides comprehensive eye care. Eye drops for treatment are available but compliance is a major challenge.

cataracts.name: Cataracts
cataracts.description: Clouding of the eye's natural lens, causing progressive blurred and dimmed vision. The leading cause of blindness in Uganda and sub-Saharan Africa — but completely treatable with a simple surgery that restores vision. Most commonly age-related but can be caused by injury, diabetes, or steroids.
cataracts.body_mechanism: The lens of the eye is normally clear — made of proteins arranged in a precise pattern. With age, UV radiation, diabetes, or malnutrition, proteins clump together, creating a cloudy area. Light passing through the cloudy lens is scattered, producing blurred, dim, or foggy vision. The cloudiness slowly worsens until the lens is completely opaque.

immediate: See an eye health worker for assessment
Cataracts are very treatable — do not resign yourself to blindness
short_term: Treatment is surgery — phacoemulsification or ECCE (extracapsular cataract extraction)
Artificial lens is inserted after removal of clouded lens
Vision is usually restored within 24-48 hours of surgery
Surgery is available and heavily subsidised in Uganda
long_term: Surgery is curative — vision typically restored to near-normal
Protect remaining eye from UV with sunglasses
Control diabetes — diabetic cataracts progress faster

see_doctor_if: Blurred vision that is worsening gradually
Glare from lights (especially at night while driving)
Vision that is hazy or foggy
White or cloudy appearance of the pupil (especially in children — needs urgent assessment)
cataracts.local_context: Cataracts cause 65% of blindness in Uganda — yet this blindness is COMPLETELY REVERSIBLE with surgery. Uganda has active cataract surgery outreach programmes. The Light for the World programme and CBM programmes perform low-cost and free cataract surgeries across Uganda. Many district hospitals now offer cataract surgery. Do not accept blindness from cataracts — seek surgery.
home_remedies: Sunglasses with UV protection slow cataract progression
Vitamin C rich foods (oranges, guava, dark leafy greens) — antioxidants slow lens clouding
Quit smoking — smokers develop cataracts 2-3 times faster

rheumatoid_arthritis.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
rheumatoid_arthritis.description: An autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the joints, causing chronic inflammation, pain, swelling, and progressive joint destruction. Unlike osteoarthritis (wear and tear), RA attacks even young people. Affects joints symmetrically and causes morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour.
rheumatoid_arthritis.body_mechanism: The immune system mistakenly attacks the synovial membrane lining of joints. This causes chronic inflammation, joint swelling, and the release of enzymes that slowly destroy cartilage and bone. The resulting joint deformity is permanent if disease is not controlled. RA also causes systemic inflammation affecting the heart, lungs, and eyes.

immediate: See a health worker — early diagnosis and treatment prevents joint destruction
Morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour in multiple joints is a red flag for RA
short_term: DMARDs (disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs) — methotrexate is first-line, prevents joint damage
NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) for pain and swelling
Low-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone) during flares
long_term: RA requires lifelong management — early treatment dramatically improves outcomes
Regular joint protection exercises — keeps joints mobile
Occupational therapy — adaptive devices for daily activities
Methotrexate available at government hospitals — requires regular blood monitoring

see_doctor_if: Pain and swelling in small joints (fingers, wrists, toes) in multiple joints
Joint stiffness worse in the morning lasting more than 1 hour
Fatigue and general illness accompanying joint symptoms
Family history of rheumatoid arthritis
rheumatoid_arthritis.local_context: Rheumatoid arthritis is underdiagnosed in Uganda and often confused with infectious arthritis or 'pains from the blood'. Rheumatology services are available at Mulago and some regional hospitals. Methotrexate, the most important treatment, is on the Uganda essential medicines list. Exercise — especially swimming and low-impact activities — is essential.
home_remedies: Fish oil (omega-3) supplements have good evidence for reducing joint inflammation in RA
Turmeric (curcumin) has anti-inflammatory properties — can complement (not replace) medication
Hot wax baths or warm water soaks for hand joints reduce morning stiffness
Gentle range-of-motion exercises daily — keeps joints mobile

sepsis.name: Sepsis (Blood Poisoning)
sepsis.description: A life-threatening emergency where the body's response to infection becomes overwhelming, damaging its own tissues and organs. Any infection — malaria, pneumonia, UTI, wound — can trigger sepsis. Kills within hours if not treated. Every minute matters.
sepsis.body_mechanism: An overwhelming infection triggers a massive, dysregulated immune response. Instead of just fighting the infection, the immune response causes widespread inflammation throughout the body. This damages blood vessel walls, allows fluid to leak from vessels, causes organs (kidney, lung, heart, brain) to fail, and the blood fails to clot properly causing dangerous bleeding.

immediate: EMERGENCY — Go to hospital immediately — sepsis kills within hours
Do not wait to see if they improve
The 'Sepsis Six' must start within 1 hour: oxygen, blood tests, IV fluids, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, monitor urine output
short_term: Hospital treatment: IV antibiotics, IV fluids, oxygen, organ support
ICU care may be needed for septic shock
Treat the source of infection
long_term: Post-sepsis syndrome: fatigue, brain fog, PTSD symptoms are common after surviving sepsis
Sepsis survivors have higher risk of future infections — stay vaccinated

see_doctor_if: High fever with confusion or altered consciousness — EMERGENCY
High fever with very fast breathing — EMERGENCY
Known infection that is rapidly worsening with signs of shock (cold skin, rapid heart rate, confusion)
Newborn or elderly person with fever and looking very unwell
sepsis.local_context: Sepsis is a major cause of death in Uganda — often from malaria, pneumonia, UTI, typhoid, or infected wounds. Recognising it early is crucial — the signs are: very high or very low temperature, fast heart rate, fast breathing, confusion. Any health facility can start treatment. Do not wait.

dvt.name: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
dvt.description: A blood clot forming in a deep vein, usually in the leg. Dangerous because clots can break off and travel to the lungs (pulmonary embolism), which can be fatal. More common than most people realise — risk increases after long travel, surgery, pregnancy, and in people who are immobile.
dvt.body_mechanism: Blood normally flows continuously through veins, but when flow slows (immobility), the vessel wall is damaged, or clotting factors are elevated (pregnancy, cancer, dehydration), a clot (thrombus) forms inside the vein. The clot partially or completely blocks blood flow, causing swelling and pain. The clot can fragment and travel through the heart to the pulmonary arteries — causing pulmonary embolism.

immediate: If sudden chest pain, breathlessness, or coughing blood after leg swelling — EMERGENCY, go to hospital now (pulmonary embolism)
Do not massage a swollen, painful leg — this can dislodge the clot
short_term: Treatment: anticoagulants (heparin then warfarin or NOAC)
Compression stockings reduce symptoms
Keep leg elevated when resting
long_term: Anticoagulation typically continues for 3-6 months minimum
Address risk factors: weight, smoking, immobility
Long-haul travel: walk every hour, stay hydrated, consider compression stockings

see_doctor_if: Swollen, painful, warm leg — especially after long travel, recent surgery, or pregnancy
Sudden breathlessness with or without chest pain
Coughing up blood with breathlessness
One leg swollen and the other normal
dvt.local_context: DVT risk is highest after long-distance travel (boda, bus, or plane) without moving, after surgery, during pregnancy, and in people who are bedridden. Warfarin for treatment requires INR blood test monitoring — available at regional hospitals. Compression stockings are available at pharmacies.

atrial_fibrillation.name: Atrial Fibrillation (AF / AFib)
atrial_fibrillation.description: An irregular, often rapid heart rhythm where the upper chambers (atria) beat chaotically instead of coordinating with the lower chambers. The most common heart rhythm disorder. Major risk factor for stroke — AF increases stroke risk by 5 times. Increasingly common in older adults.
atrial_fibrillation.body_mechanism: Disorganised electrical signals in the atria cause them to quiver rather than pump effectively. This allows blood to pool in the atria, where clots can form. Clots can then travel to the brain causing stroke. The chaotic rhythm causes palpitations, fatigue, and breathlessness. Over time, uncontrolled AF damages heart muscle.

immediate: If sudden irregular rapid heartbeat with chest pain or breathlessness — go to hospital
ECG (electrocardiogram) confirms the diagnosis
short_term: Rate control medication: beta-blockers (atenolol) or digoxin to slow heart rate
Anticoagulants (warfarin) to prevent stroke — the most important treatment
Treat underlying causes: hypertension, thyroid disease, alcohol
long_term: AF management is usually lifelong
Strict blood pressure control reduces AF burden
Avoid alcohol — a major trigger and worsener of AF
Regular INR monitoring if on warfarin — available at government hospitals

see_doctor_if: Palpitations that are irregular (not just fast but irregular)
Palpitations with dizziness, breathlessness, or chest pain
Sudden one-sided weakness, facial droop, or speech difficulty — this may be a stroke from AF
You are over 65 with hypertension — get ECG
atrial_fibrillation.local_context: Atrial fibrillation is underdiagnosed in Uganda. It is a major cause of stroke. Rheumatic heart disease (from untreated strep throat in childhood) is a common cause of AF in young Ugandans. Digoxin and atenolol for rate control are on the Uganda essential medicines list. ECG machines are available at all hospitals.
home_remedies: Stop alcohol completely — alcohol is the single biggest modifiable trigger of AF
Control blood pressure rigorously
Maintain healthy weight — obesity is a major AF driver
Reduce caffeine if it triggers palpitations

neonatal_jaundice.name: Neonatal Jaundice (Newborn Yellowing)
neonatal_jaundice.description: Yellowing of a newborn's skin and eyes in the first few days of life, caused by elevated bilirubin. Very common and usually harmless (physiological jaundice). However, severe jaundice can cause permanent brain damage (kernicterus) — recognition and treatment is essential.
neonatal_jaundice.body_mechanism: Newborns have high red blood cell counts at birth that break down rapidly, releasing bilirubin. The immature newborn liver cannot conjugate and excrete bilirubin fast enough, so it builds up in blood and deposits in skin (yellow colour) and eyes. Usually peaks at day 3-5 then resolves. Pathological jaundice (due to blood group incompatibility, infection, or liver disease) appears earlier and rises more rapidly.

immediate: Any newborn with yellow skin in first 24 hours of life — go to hospital URGENTLY (pathological)
Yellow skin + poor feeding + lethargy = URGENT — hospital now
For mild jaundice appearing after 24 hours: frequent feeding (8-12 times/day) helps clear bilirubin
short_term: Phototherapy (blue light treatment) breaks down bilirubin — available at most hospitals
Frequent breastfeeding is both treatment and prevention — ensures bilirubin is excreted in stool
Blood test (bilirubin level) determines severity and whether phototherapy is needed
long_term: Physiological jaundice resolves within 2 weeks with no long-term effects
Follow up if baby remains yellow beyond 2 weeks — may indicate liver disease

see_doctor_if: Yellow skin appearing in first 24 hours of life
Yellowing spreading to arms, legs, or palms/soles
Baby is difficult to wake or very lethargic
Baby is feeding poorly
Jaundice still present after 2 weeks
Baby has high-pitched cry, arching of back, or eye movements (signs of bilirubin toxicity)
neonatal_jaundice.local_context: Neonatal jaundice is very common in Uganda. Phototherapy units are available at health centre IVs and hospitals. Traditional practices of 'sunning' babies (direct sunlight exposure) can help mild cases but are not sufficient for significant jaundice — seek medical assessment. Do not delay if baby looks very yellow.
home_remedies: Frequent breastfeeding (every 1-2 hours) helps flush bilirubin through stools
Indirect sunlight through a window (not direct sun which can burn) may help mild physiological jaundice
Never use herbal preparations on a jaundiced newborn — can worsen liver function

croup.name: Croup
croup.description: A viral infection in young children causing inflammation and narrowing of the larynx (voice box) and trachea (windpipe). Characterised by a distinctive 'barking seal' cough and harsh breathing sounds (stridor). Most common in children aged 6 months to 3 years. Usually mild but can cause significant breathing difficulty.
croup.body_mechanism: Viruses (usually parainfluenza) inflame and swell the area just below the vocal cords. Because young children have narrow airways, even small swelling significantly reduces airflow. The barking cough is caused by air moving through the narrowed area. Stridor (harsh breathing sound) occurs when the obstruction is significant.

immediate: If child has severe breathing difficulty, drooling, or looks blue — hospital IMMEDIATELY
Stay calm — anxiety makes breathing harder for the child
Cool night air can relieve mild croup — take child outside or open window
short_term: Dexamethasone (oral or injection) given at health facility significantly reduces swelling
Nebulised adrenaline in hospital for severe cases
Keep child upright — lying flat worsens breathing
Cool mist from a humidifier or cool bathroom may help
long_term: Most cases resolve within 3-5 days
Croup tends to recur in susceptible children — parents learn to recognise it quickly

see_doctor_if: Stridor (noisy breathing) at rest
Child is working hard to breathe (ribs visible with each breath)
Child looks blue or pale
Drooling or unable to swallow (may be epiglottitis — different and more dangerous)
Child is very agitated or very sleepy from breathing effort
croup.local_context: Croup is common in Uganda, particularly in cooler months. The barking cough is very distinctive — parents who have heard it once recognise it immediately. Dexamethasone for treatment is on the Uganda essential medicines list and available at health centres. Most mild cases can be managed at home with cool air, but any child with breathing difficulty at rest needs hospital assessment.
home_remedies: Cool night air — often dramatically relieves mild croup symptoms within minutes
Keep child calm and upright
Cool mist from a wet cloth or bowl of cool water in the room may help
Do NOT use steam — can cause scalding and may worsen symptoms

otitis_media.name: Otitis Media (Middle Ear Infection)
otitis_media.description: Infection of the middle ear — the space behind the eardrum. Extremely common in children. Causes ear pain, fever, and hearing loss. A leading cause of preventable hearing loss in Uganda when recurrent and untreated.
otitis_media.body_mechanism: Bacteria or viruses from upper respiratory tract infection travel up the Eustachian tube (connecting throat to middle ear) and infect the middle ear space. Pus accumulates, building pressure against the eardrum — causing pain. The eardrum may perforate (burst), releasing pus — paradoxically, perforation relieves pain. Repeated infections and perforations damage hearing structures.

immediate: Pain relief with paracetamol or ibuprofen
See health worker — most cases need antibiotics (amoxicillin)
Warm compress against the ear reduces pain
short_term: Complete the full antibiotic course — even when pain resolves
Follow up in 2-4 weeks to confirm resolution
If ear is discharging, keep dry — no water in ear
long_term: Children with recurrent ear infections (3+ per year) need ENT specialist assessment
Hearing test after repeated infections
Grommets (tiny ventilation tubes) may be needed for recurrent cases
Breastfeeding protects against ear infections — promotes Eustachian tube function

see_doctor_if: Ear pain in a child with fever
Child pulling or rubbing ear
Ear discharge (pus or blood)
Hearing seems reduced after infection
Swelling behind the ear — could indicate mastoiditis (serious complication)
otitis_media.local_context: Ear infections are a major cause of preventable hearing loss and deafness in Ugandan children, often due to untreated acute infections. Amoxicillin is first-line treatment and available at all health facilities. Children in Uganda's refugee settlements have particularly high rates. Hearing impairment from repeated ear infections significantly affects school performance.
home_remedies: Warm compress against the outer ear reduces pain
Keep ear dry — avoid water entering the ear canal during infection
Breastfeed infants for as long as possible — dramatically reduces ear infection frequency
Avoid smoking near children — cigarette smoke increases ear infection risk 3-fold

psoriasis.name: Psoriasis
psoriasis.description: A chronic autoimmune skin condition causing rapid overproduction of skin cells, forming red, thick, scaly patches. Not contagious. Affects 2-3% of people globally. Comes in flares and remissions. Associated with increased risk of psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular disease, and depression.
psoriasis.body_mechanism: The immune system mistakenly attacks skin cells, triggering them to divide every 3-4 days instead of the normal 28-30 days. These excess cells pile up on the skin surface, forming the characteristic thick, silvery-scaled plaques. The inflammatory process also affects joints in some people (psoriatic arthritis) and increases cardiovascular inflammation.

immediate: See a health worker for diagnosis — confirm it is psoriasis (not eczema, ringworm, or other skin conditions)
Moisturise affected areas frequently — reduces scaling and discomfort
short_term: Topical treatments: corticosteroid creams (betamethasone), coal tar preparations, Vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol)
Sunlight exposure (controlled) improves most psoriasis — UV light slows skin cell division
Avoid triggers: stress, alcohol, skin trauma, certain medications
long_term: Severe cases: phototherapy (medically controlled UV light), systemic treatments (methotrexate)
Methotrexate is very effective for severe psoriasis and available at regional hospitals
Psoriasis is chronic — good management reduces flares significantly

see_doctor_if: Extensive red, scaly patches over large body areas
Psoriasis covering more than 10% of body
Joint pain associated with skin disease (psoriatic arthritis)
Sudden widespread rash after illness (guttate psoriasis)
Painful, cracked skin that bleeds
psoriasis.local_context: Psoriasis is often misdiagnosed as a fungal infection in Uganda and treated inappropriately with antifungals. It is not contagious and not caused by poor hygiene. Dermatological care is available at regional hospitals. Betamethasone cream is widely available. Avoiding alcohol and managing stress significantly reduces flares.
home_remedies: Controlled sun exposure (avoid sunburn) — UV light reduces psoriasis activity
Aloe vera gel applied to plaques — soothes inflammation and reduces scaling
Coconut oil as moisturiser — reduces scaling and prevents skin cracking
Oatmeal baths reduce itching and inflammation
Turmeric (applied or consumed) — anti-inflammatory properties may reduce plaques

ringworm_tinea.name: Ringworm (Tinea / Fungal Skin Infection)
ringworm_tinea.description: A very common fungal infection of the skin causing ring-shaped, scaly, itchy patches. Despite the name, it is NOT caused by a worm. Spreads through skin contact, shared clothing, or contact with infected animals. Completely treatable with antifungal cream.
ringworm_tinea.body_mechanism: Dermatophyte fungi (Trichophyton, Microsporum species) infect the dead outer layers of skin, hair, and nails — they cannot survive in living tissue. They produce enzymes that digest keratin (the protein in skin and hair). As they spread outward from a central point, the centre clears while the advancing edge remains active — creating the characteristic ring appearance.

immediate: Apply clotrimazole or miconazole antifungal cream twice daily
Keep affected area clean and dry
Do not share towels, combs, or clothing
short_term: Continue antifungal cream for 2 weeks after the rash clears — stopping early causes relapse
For scalp ringworm (tinea capitis): oral antifungal (griseofulvin or fluconazole) — cream alone doesn't work for scalp
Wash all clothing and bedding that contacted the rash
long_term: Prevent reinfection: keep skin dry, dry thoroughly between toes, don't share personal items
Treat pets with ringworm — they are a common source of reinfection

see_doctor_if: Rash not improving after 2 weeks of antifungal cream
Scalp infection with hair loss — needs oral antifungal
Nail infection — needs oral antifungal (cream cannot penetrate nails)
Spreading rash in a person with diabetes or weakened immune system
ringworm_tinea.local_context: Ringworm is extremely common in Uganda, particularly in children sharing bedding in schools and boarding facilities. Clotrimazole cream is cheap and available at all pharmacies. Scalp ringworm causing hair loss in children (tinea capitis) requires oral griseofulvin — available at health centres. Confirm it's ringworm rather than psoriasis or eczema before treating.
home_remedies: Tea tree oil has antifungal properties — dilute with carrier oil and apply twice daily
Garlic has proven antifungal effects — crush and apply to affected area (test on small area first — can cause skin irritation)
Keep skin dry — fungi grow in moisture; dry thoroughly after bathing
Apple cider vinegar (diluted 1:1 with water) applied to the rash — creates hostile environment for fungi

schistosomiasis.name: Schistosomiasis (Bilharzia)
schistosomiasis.description: A parasitic worm infection caused by Schistosoma blood flukes, contracted by contact with contaminated fresh water. One of Uganda's most prevalent diseases, affecting millions especially around Lake Victoria, Lake Albert, and Lake Edward. Chronic infection damages the liver, bladder, and intestines silently over years.
schistosomiasis.body_mechanism: Schistosome larvae (cercariae) penetrate bare skin during contact with infected lake, river, or pond water. They migrate through the bloodstream to mature into adult worms in blood vessels around the intestines or bladder. The worms lay thousands of eggs — some pass out in urine or stool, but many lodge in organs, causing chronic immune-driven inflammation, fibrosis (scarring), and organ damage.
schistosomiasis.why_symptoms: Early infection (Katayama fever) causes fever, rash, and body aches as the immune system reacts to the migrating larvae. Chronic intestinal schistosomiasis causes abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea, and liver/spleen enlargement as egg deposits accumulate. Urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium) causes blood in urine (haematuria), bladder damage, and increased risk of bladder cancer and female infertility.

immediate: Get tested at a health facility — urine microscopy (blood in urine), stool microscopy, or a rapid antibody test
Single dose praziquantel (40mg/kg) cures most infections — highly effective
Do not delay — years of untreated infection cause permanent liver and bladder scarring
Take paracetamol for fever and body aches
short_term: After treatment: have a follow-up urine or stool test at 6 weeks to confirm clearance
Reinfection is very common — prevent re-exposure: avoid swimming or wading in Lake Victoria, Lake Albert, or other fresh water bodies in affected areas
Treat iron deficiency anaemia if present
Educate household members — if one person is infected, others in the family likely are too
Children in affected areas should participate in school-based mass drug administration (MDA) campaigns
long_term: Annual praziquantel during MDA campaigns in endemic areas is recommended for school-age children
Protect from reinfection: use clean treated water for bathing where possible
Monitor for liver and bladder complications with annual check-up in heavily-infected individuals
In Uganda: bilharzia is endemic in lakeshore communities — Lake Victoria, Lake Albert, Lake George, Lake Edward, and rivers flowing from highlands

see_doctor_if: Blood in urine or stool
Swollen abdomen (liver or spleen enlargement)
Severe anaemia
Child with growth retardation and school performance decline in a bilharzia-endemic area
Neurological symptoms (rare — spinal cord involvement)
schistosomiasis.local_context: Uganda has one of the highest schistosomiasis burdens in the world. Approximately 3-4 million Ugandans are infected. Endemic in all lakeshore and riverine communities: Lake Victoria shores (Jinja, Entebbe, Masaka, Busia areas), Lake Albert (Hoima, Buliisa), Kagera River basin, and western Uganda. The MOH and NDA conduct periodic mass drug administration (MDA) campaigns providing free praziquantel to school children. Adults in endemic areas should access testing and treatment at health centres.
home_remedies: None effective against schistosomiasis — praziquantel from a health facility is essential

sickle_cell_disease.name: Sickle Cell Disease (SCD)
sickle_cell_disease.description: A serious inherited blood disorder where red blood cells become abnormally shaped (sickle-shaped) causing them to block blood vessels, break down quickly, and deliver less oxygen to the body. Uganda has one of the highest prevalences of sickle cell disease in the world — approximately 20,000 children are born with SCD annually in Uganda.
sickle_cell_disease.body_mechanism: People with SCD have inherited an abnormal haemoglobin gene (HbS) from both parents (HbSS is the most severe form). The abnormal haemoglobin causes red blood cells to become rigid and sickle-shaped under conditions of low oxygen, dehydration, cold, infection, or stress. These sickled cells block small blood vessels, cutting off blood supply to organs and causing intense pain (vaso-occlusive crisis) and progressive organ damage.
sickle_cell_disease.why_symptoms: Painful crises occur when sickled cells block vessels in bones, joints, chest, and abdomen. Chronic anaemia occurs because sickled cells are destroyed in 10-20 days (vs 120 days for normal cells). The spleen is damaged early in life — children become vulnerable to serious bacterial infections (malaria, pneumococcal infections, salmonella). The liver, kidneys, eyes, and brain are progressively damaged by repeated vessel blockage.

immediate: Painful crisis: Drink large amounts of fluids (water, juice) immediately — dehydration worsens sickling
Take strong pain medication (ibuprofen, paracetamol, or if prescribed — codeine) promptly
Apply warm (not hot) cloths to the painful area
Go to hospital if pain is not controlled at home, fever is present, or breathing is difficult
Acute chest syndrome (chest pain + fever + breathing difficulty) = EMERGENCY — go to hospital immediately
Stroke symptoms (sudden weakness, speech problems) = EMERGENCY
short_term: Register at a sickle cell disease clinic — Mulago SCD clinic, Jinja Referral, or regional SCD clinic
Daily hydroxyurea treatment (from age 6 months) reduces crises by 50% and prevents organ damage — ask your health provider
Folic acid 5mg daily — SCD patients need extra folate for rapid cell turnover
Penicillin V prophylaxis in children under 5 to prevent bacterial infections
Malaria prevention is critical — use insecticide-treated nets every night, antimalarial prophylaxis where recommended
Pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae vaccination
long_term: Annual eye checks (retinal damage from SCD)
Annual kidney function tests
Annual transcranial Doppler ultrasound in children (detects stroke risk)
Blood transfusions if severely anaemic, before surgery, or after stroke
Genetic counselling for family planning — if both parents carry sickle cell trait, 25% chance of SCD in child
Uganda has free newborn sickle cell screening at some centres — all newborns should be tested if family history or in high-prevalence areas

see_doctor_if: Fever above 38.5°C — can be life-threatening in SCD (functional asplenia)
Chest pain with breathing difficulty (acute chest syndrome)
Any stroke symptoms
Severe pain not controlled at home
Prolonged painful erection (priapism)
Sudden vision changes or eye pain
Severe anaemia (very pale, extremely tired, rapid heart rate)
sickle_cell_disease.local_context: Uganda has approximately 20,000 new SCD births annually — one of the world's highest burdens. Sickle cell trait (carrier state) is present in 13-20% of Ugandans in some areas. Free or subsidised SCD care is available at Mulago National Referral Hospital's SCD clinic (one of East Africa's largest), Jinja Referral Hospital, and regional hospitals. The Uganda Sickle Cell Rescue Foundation also provides support and community education. Hydroxyurea is increasingly available through the MOH programme. The Sickle Cell Disease Association of Uganda can connect families with resources.
home_remedies: Warm compresses for joint/bone pain during crisis
Hydration — drink as much as possible during crisis
Rest during painful crisis
Folic acid-rich foods: beans, green vegetables, liver

pre_eclampsia.name: Pre-Eclampsia and Eclampsia
pre_eclampsia.description: Pre-eclampsia is a dangerous pregnancy complication characterised by high blood pressure and organ damage (especially kidneys and liver) after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Eclampsia is pre-eclampsia with seizures (convulsions). Together they are Uganda's leading cause of maternal death, killing more Ugandan mothers than any other single complication.
pre_eclampsia.body_mechanism: Pre-eclampsia starts with abnormal placental blood vessel development. The placenta releases factors into the mother's bloodstream that cause widespread blood vessel damage. This results in high blood pressure, protein leaking through damaged kidney filters into urine, liver damage, low platelet counts, and in the most severe cases — seizures (eclampsia), stroke, placental abruption, and multi-organ failure.
pre_eclampsia.why_symptoms: High blood pressure damages blood vessels throughout the body. Protein in urine indicates kidney damage. Severe headache signals brain vessel involvement (warning of impending seizure). Visual disturbances (flashing lights, blurred vision) indicate retinal vessel involvement. Upper abdominal pain under the ribs indicates liver swelling. Sudden leg swelling beyond normal pregnancy. Any seizure in a pregnant woman after 20 weeks is eclampsia until proven otherwise.

immediate: ECLAMPSIA (SEIZURES IN PREGNANT WOMAN) = ABSOLUTE EMERGENCY — Call for help, get to hospital IMMEDIATELY
Do NOT leave a seizing pregnant woman alone — roll to left side to protect airway
If available: give Magnesium Sulphate (standard protocol — health workers only)
Any pregnant woman with severe headache, visual disturbances, or upper abdominal pain: go to hospital immediately — do not wait
If blood pressure reading is ≥160/110 or higher: hospital emergency — same day
Do NOT attempt to control seizure with diazepam without magnesium sulphate — magnesium is superior
short_term: All pregnant women should attend antenatal care (ANC) — blood pressure checked every visit is how pre-eclampsia is caught early
Uganda ANC protocol: 4+ visits minimum — attend at 4 months, 6 months, 8 months, and once more before delivery
Calcium supplementation (1.5g/day) from 20 weeks reduces risk of pre-eclampsia by 50% in high-risk women
Low-dose aspirin (75-100mg) from 12-16 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia risk in high-risk women (first pregnancy, previous pre-eclampsia, twins, hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease)
Know the danger signs and go to health facility SAME DAY
long_term: After pre-eclampsia: 20-30% recurrence risk in future pregnancies
Women who had pre-eclampsia have higher lifetime risk of hypertension, stroke, and heart disease — annual blood pressure checks
Breastfeeding reduces long-term cardiovascular risk after pre-eclampsia
Space pregnancies at least 2 years apart

see_doctor_if: ANY seizure during pregnancy or up to 6 weeks after delivery — EMERGENCY
Severe headache that does not improve with paracetamol (especially after 20 weeks)
Flashing lights or sudden visual changes during pregnancy
Swelling of face or hands (beyond normal ankle swelling)
Pain in upper abdomen under right rib cage during pregnancy
Very little urine output during pregnancy
Blood pressure ≥140/90 at any antenatal visit
pre_eclampsia.local_context: Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia account for approximately 10-15% of maternal deaths in Uganda — making it the top direct cause of maternal mortality. Uganda has one of the world's highest rates. Many deaths are preventable through ANC attendance, early detection, and emergency treatment with magnesium sulphate. All government health centres and above stock magnesium sulphate. Low calcium intake (common in Uganda) is a major risk factor — calcium-rich foods (groundnuts, beans, dagaa fish, dark green vegetables, sim sim) should be prioritised in pregnancy. Calcium supplements are provided free in ANC in many facilities.
home_remedies: No home treatment — pre-eclampsia and eclampsia are medical emergencies. Seek care immediately. Calcium-rich foods during pregnancy may help prevention.

postpartum_depression.name: Postpartum Depression (PPD) / Postnatal Depression
postpartum_depression.description: A serious mental health condition that can affect women (and sometimes men) after childbirth. Much more than 'baby blues' — postpartum depression involves persistent sadness, inability to bond with baby, and significant impairment. Affects 15-20% of new mothers in Uganda. Commonly missed and undertreated due to stigma.
postpartum_depression.body_mechanism: After delivery, oestrogen and progesterone levels drop dramatically. This rapid hormonal change, combined with sleep deprivation, physical recovery, new responsibilities, and sometimes a difficult birth or baby, can trigger depression in vulnerable women. The brain's mood-regulating chemistry (serotonin, dopamine) is disrupted. Additional risk factors in Uganda: partner violence, poverty, lack of support, previous mental illness, complicated delivery, stillbirth or unwell baby.
postpartum_depression.why_symptoms: Sadness, crying, and hopelessness come from disrupted brain chemistry. Difficulty bonding with baby stems from neurobiological disruption of maternal attachment circuits. Anxiety and panic about baby's safety are common. Sleep problems (beyond normal infant care waking) involve hyperarousal of the stress system. Thoughts of harming oneself or baby (in severe cases) require urgent psychiatric attention.

immediate: Talk to someone you trust today — a spouse, sister, mother, or friend
You are NOT a bad mother — PPD is a medical condition, not a weakness or sign of failure
Attend your postnatal clinic visit — tell the midwife or health worker how you are feeling
If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby — go to hospital today, or call a trusted person to stay with you
short_term: Mental health counselling (talk therapy) — effective and available at some health facilities in Uganda
For moderate to severe PPD — antidepressant medication may be needed and is safe with breastfeeding (sertraline is preferred)
Involve your partner — they need to understand PPD to provide support
Accept practical help from family — with childcare, cooking, other children
Rest when baby sleeps — sleep deprivation worsens depression
Eat regular nutritious meals — poor nutrition worsens mood
long_term: PPD is treatable — most women recover fully with support and treatment
The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a screening tool used in some Ugandan facilities
Previous PPD: high risk of recurrence — plan for support and early treatment in future pregnancies
Postpartum psychosis (much rarer — 1 in 1000) involves hallucinations, delusions, very rapid onset after delivery = psychiatric emergency

see_doctor_if: Feeling deeply sad or hopeless for more than 2 weeks after birth
Unable to care for yourself or your baby
Not bonding with your baby after several weeks
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby — EMERGENCY
Hearing or seeing things others cannot (postpartum psychosis) — EMERGENCY
postpartum_depression.local_context: Postpartum depression is common in Uganda but rarely diagnosed due to stigma, lack of screening, and cultural expectations that a new mother should be happy. Research shows 15-25% of Ugandan mothers experience significant postpartum depression. Risk factors prevalent in Uganda: partner violence (very common), poverty, lack of partner support, young mothers, complicated deliveries, stillbirth. Butabika Hospital (national psychiatric hospital) and some regional hospitals have mental health services. Community Health Workers (VHTs) can be a bridge to mental health care. Cultural practices in some communities restrict a new mother's movement — while some support is helpful, isolation without support is harmful.
home_remedies: Social support — do not be alone
Gentle physical activity as able after delivery
Regular meals
Accept practical help
Prayer and spiritual support if meaningful to you — but also seek medical help, not only spiritual

malnutrition_sam.name: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in Children
malnutrition_sam.description: The most severe and life-threatening form of malnutrition, primarily in children under 5 years. Uganda has significant SAM burden especially in Karamoja, West Nile, and other food-insecure regions. A child with SAM has a greatly increased risk of dying from infection, and the condition causes permanent brain and physical development damage if untreated.
malnutrition_sam.body_mechanism: When a child receives severely insufficient protein and energy, the body progressively breaks down muscle and fat stores to survive. The immune system becomes severely impaired. The gut lining deteriorates, making it impossible to absorb even available food. The heart weakens. The liver fails to produce essential proteins. Electrolyte balances are critically disrupted. Every organ system is affected. The child becomes increasingly unable to fight any infection.
malnutrition_sam.why_symptoms: Severe wasting (visible ribs, thin limbs, hollow cheeks) occurs as muscle and fat are consumed. The MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference) below 11.5cm in children 6-59 months is the standard diagnostic tool. Marasmus (severe wasting) appears as a 'little old person'. Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency) shows as fluid-filled swelling (oedema) in the feet, legs, face — giving a deceptively chubby appearance. Hair becomes thin and reddish. Skin peels. The child is miserable, crying weakly or abnormally quiet.

immediate: A child with SAM needs hospital or therapeutic feeding centre care — this is a medical emergency
Check for medical complications: if child has fever, pneumonia, severe diarrhoea, or very low blood sugar — take to hospital now
If child is alert and can eat: Plumpy'Nut (RUTF — Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food) from a health facility is the treatment for uncomplicated SAM
Do not give sugar water — this can cause dangerous electrolyte imbalance
Give small amounts of breastmilk or F-75 therapeutic milk (hospital) frequently
short_term: RUTF (Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food — Plumpy'Nut) is available FREE at most health centres and hospitals in Uganda
Community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) allows uncomplicated SAM to be treated at home with RUTF
Weekly health facility visits for monitoring during CMAM treatment — 6-8 weeks average course
Treat complicating infections (malaria, pneumonia, TB) simultaneously
Vitamin A, folic acid, zinc supplementation
All household members assessed — sibling malnutrition common
long_term: Supplementary feeding for moderate malnutrition (MAM) — 11.5-12.5cm MUAC
IMAM programme (Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition) — Uganda health system
Underlying causes: food insecurity, poverty, poor feeding practices, recurrent infection, large family size — address through VHT and community level
Growth monitoring at every health visit (weighing children monthly under 2 years)
Optimal breastfeeding: exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months, then complementary foods with continued breastfeeding to 2 years

see_doctor_if: Any child under 5 who looks severely thin or has swelling in feet and face
Child with MUAC below 11.5cm (red zone on MUAC tape)
Child who refuses all food or drink
Any severely malnourished child with fever, difficulty breathing, or diarrhoea
Child who is very drowsy or unresponsive
malnutrition_sam.local_context: Uganda has approximately 1.2 million children under 5 suffering from acute malnutrition at any given time, with SAM affecting around 200,000. Karamoja region has the highest rates (up to 30% of children acutely malnourished). RUTF (Plumpy'Nut) is available FREE at health centres III and above across Uganda. Uganda's IMAM programme is one of sub-Saharan Africa's largest. VHTs (Village Health Teams) conduct community screening using MUAC tapes. The UNCHR and WFP operate supplementary feeding programmes in refugee settlements. Underlying causes include food insecurity, recurrent malaria, poor water and sanitation, and large family size.
home_remedies: RUTF (Plumpy'Nut) from health facility — this IS the home treatment for uncomplicated SAM
Continued breastfeeding
Oral Rehydration Solution if diarrhoea present

giardiasis.name: Giardiasis (Giardia)
giardiasis.description: A common intestinal infection caused by the microscopic parasite Giardia intestinalis (also called Giardia lamblia), spread through contaminated water and food. A significant cause of chronic diarrhoea and malnutrition in Uganda, especially in children.
giardiasis.body_mechanism: Giardia cysts are ingested in contaminated water, raw vegetables washed in contaminated water, or from the hands of infected people. The cysts transform into active trophozoites in the small intestine, where they attach to the intestinal lining. This disrupts fat and nutrient absorption, causing fatty diarrhoea, bloating, and malabsorption. The condition can become chronic if untreated.
giardiasis.why_symptoms: Watery or greasy (fatty, pale, difficult to flush) diarrhoea results from disrupted fat absorption. Bloating and excessive gas occur from fermentation of undigested food. Burping with an unpleasant 'rotten egg' smell is characteristic. Abdominal cramps, nausea, and fatigue are typical. Notably: Giardia does NOT cause fever or blood in stool (unlike bacterial infections — if fever or blood present, consider other diagnoses).

immediate: Take metronidazole 400mg three times daily for 5 days (adults) — highly effective
For children: metronidazole 15mg/kg three times daily for 5 days
Tinidazole 2g single dose is an alternative for adults
Drink boiled or treated water only during treatment and afterwards
Rigorous handwashing after toilet use and before meals
short_term: Improve water treatment: boil drinking water for 1 minute, or use water purification tablets
Wash all fruits and vegetables with treated water
Treat all household members if multiple people have symptoms — person-to-person spread
Avoid swimming in potentially contaminated fresh water sources
long_term: In children: assess for malnutrition if weight is not recovering — Giardia causes significant malabsorption
Recurrence is common with continued contaminated water exposure
Zinc supplementation may help recovery of gut lining

see_doctor_if: Diarrhoea lasting more than 2 weeks
Significant weight loss
Blood or mucus in stool (consider other diagnoses)
Fever (uncommon in Giardia — reconsider diagnosis)
Child with failure to thrive or growth faltering
giardiasis.local_context: Giardiasis is endemic in Uganda, particularly in areas with poor water and sanitation. Contaminated water sources, lack of latrines, and hand hygiene gaps drive transmission. Particularly affects children in schools and densely populated areas. Metronidazole is available at all health centres in Uganda and is inexpensive.
home_remedies: Boiled or treated water
Good handwashing
Oral rehydration salt (ORS) solution if dehydrated

brucellosis.name: Brucellosis (Undulant Fever)
brucellosis.description: A bacterial infection acquired from infected animals or their products — raw milk, undercooked meat, or direct animal contact. Uganda has significant brucellosis burden especially in cattle-keeping communities (Ankole, Karamoja, Teso, Lango sub-regions).
brucellosis.body_mechanism: Brucella bacteria enter the body through the digestive tract (raw milk or meat), breaks in skin (contact with animal tissue), eyes, or inhalation. The bacteria spread to lymph nodes, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and joints where they survive inside immune cells and trigger chronic inflammation. Characteristically causes 'undulant fever' — fever that rises in waves over days.
brucellosis.why_symptoms: Undulant fever (rising and falling in waves) is characteristic. Profuse drenching sweats, especially at night. Deep bone and joint pain — particularly in the spine, hips, and knees. Fatigue is extreme and persistent. Headache. Enlarged liver and spleen. In men, orchitis (testicular inflammation) is a classic complication. Complications of chronic disease: spondylitis (spine infection), endocarditis, meningitis, hepatitis.

immediate: See a health provider for blood tests (brucellosis serology, blood culture)
Treatment requires 6 weeks of dual antibiotic therapy: Doxycycline 100mg twice daily PLUS Rifampicin 600-900mg once daily for 6 weeks
Do not treat with only one antibiotic — high relapse rate
Take complete course — stopping early leads to relapse and potentially life-threatening complications
short_term: Stop consuming raw milk or undercooked meat from animals
Pasteurise or boil milk before drinking
Alert your livestock vet — brucellosis in your herd can be addressed through veterinary intervention
Report to your district veterinary officer — brucellosis is a notifiable disease in Uganda
long_term: Vaccination of cattle reduces human cases — veterinary programmes
Avoid direct contact with animal placenta, aborted fetuses, or birth fluids without protective gear
Cook meat thoroughly
Cattle herding communities should be aware of brucellosis symptoms

see_doctor_if: Fever that lasts more than 2 weeks in a cattle-keeping community
Severe back pain with fever (spinal involvement)
Testicular swelling with fever (orchitis)
Neurological symptoms with fever
brucellosis.local_context: Brucellosis is a significant but underdiagnosed disease in Uganda's cattle-keeping regions: Ankole (Mbarara, Bushenyi), Karamoja (Moroto, Kotido), Teso (Soroti), and Lango. Consumption of raw milk ('ejuma' — raw milk mixed in tea or food in Ankole) is a major transmission route. Brucellosis is also an occupational risk for veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers, and farmers. Doxycycline and rifampicin are available at district hospitals.
home_remedies: Boil all milk before drinking
Cook meat thoroughly
No effective home treatment for established infection — medical treatment essential

febrile_convulsions.name: Febrile Convulsions (Fever-Related Seizures in Children)
febrile_convulsions.description: Seizures (convulsions/fits) triggered by high fever in children aged 6 months to 5 years. Very common — affects 2-5% of all children. Usually brief and not causing brain damage. Frightening for parents but typically benign, though immediate care is needed to rule out serious causes like meningitis or malaria.
febrile_convulsions.body_mechanism: Young children's brains are more sensitive to temperature changes than adult brains. A rapidly rising fever lowers the seizure threshold — the electrical threshold at which brain cells fire abnormally. The fever itself (not the height alone) triggers synchronised abnormal electrical activity across the brain, causing a convulsion. Most febrile convulsions are 'simple' — lasting under 15 minutes, affecting the whole body, occurring once in 24 hours. Complex febrile convulsions are longer, one-sided, or recur within 24 hours.
febrile_convulsions.why_symptoms: The seizure causes stiff limbs, jerking movements, rolling eyes, unconsciousness, and possibly breath-holding or turning blue briefly. Bladder or bowel loss may occur. After the seizure, the child is deeply drowsy for 10-60 minutes (post-ictal period). A fever is present (though it may have been high and dropped by the time you notice the convulsion).

immediate: STAY CALM — most febrile convulsions stop on their own within 1-3 minutes
Protect from injury: lay child on their side (recovery position) on a flat safe surface, cushion head
DO NOT put anything in the mouth — this is dangerous and not necessary
DO NOT hold the child down forcibly
Time the seizure — if it goes beyond 5 minutes, this is an emergency needing diazepam
After the seizure stops: keep child on side, give paracetamol for fever (suppository if available, otherwise oral once child is swallowing)
GO TO HEALTH FACILITY after any febrile convulsion — malaria, meningitis, and other serious causes must be excluded
short_term: At health facility: blood test for malaria (rapid test), check for signs of meningitis (neck stiffness, fontanelle), lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected
Treat the underlying fever cause
Keep child cool during fevers: remove excess clothing, tepid sponging, paracetamol/ibuprofen
Simple febrile convulsions: no long-term anticonvulsant medication needed
Recurrence risk: 30% of children will have another febrile convulsion with subsequent fevers
long_term: Simple febrile convulsions do NOT cause epilepsy or brain damage — reassure parents
Teach parents seizure first aid — they need to know what to do for the next episode
Complex febrile convulsions (prolonged, one-sided, multiple in 24 hours): need paediatric neurology follow-up
Febrile seizures usually stop by age 5-6 years as brain matures

see_doctor_if: ALL febrile convulsions need health facility assessment — same day
Seizure lasting more than 5 minutes — EMERGENCY — give diazepam (health worker)
Multiple seizures in same illness
Child does not recover consciousness after 30-60 minutes
Neck stiffness or bulging fontanelle with fever (meningitis)
Child under 6 months or over 5 years with fever seizure (not typical febrile convulsion age)
febrile_convulsions.local_context: Febrile convulsions are very common in Uganda, where fevers from malaria are frequent. In malaria-endemic Uganda, cerebral malaria must be excluded in any child with fever and seizure — cerebral malaria is a life-threatening emergency. Health facility assessment after any febrile convulsion is mandatory. Diazepam rectal solution or diazepam suppositories should ideally be available in communities where children have had complex or prolonged febrile convulsions.
home_remedies: Recovery position during seizure
Paracetamol for fever control after seizure
Tepid sponging to reduce fever
No other home management — seek health care immediately after any seizure

acute_bronchitis.name: Acute Bronchitis / Acute Cough
acute_bronchitis.description: Inflammation of the bronchial tubes (airways leading to the lungs) usually caused by a viral infection. The main symptom is a cough — dry at first, sometimes becoming productive. Very common and self-limiting, usually resolving in 2–3 weeks.
acute_bronchitis.body_mechanism: A virus (most commonly rhinovirus, influenza, or RSV) infects the lining of the bronchial tubes. Your immune system triggers inflammation and mucus production to trap and expel the virus. This causes the cough reflex to fire repeatedly. The cough may persist for 2–3 weeks even after the infection clears, because the bronchial lining takes time to heal.

immediate: Rest — your immune system needs energy to fight the infection
Drink plenty of warm fluids — thins mucus and soothes airways
Honey in warm water or tea — reduces cough frequency (as effective as cough syrup)
Steam inhalation for 10 minutes — opens airways and loosens mucus
Avoid smoke, dust, and cooking fumes — worsens bronchial inflammation
short_term: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever or chest soreness — not for the cough itself
Do NOT take antibiotics — acute bronchitis is almost always viral
Over-the-counter cough suppressants have limited evidence but can help at night
Most acute coughs resolve within 2-3 weeks without treatment
Salbutamol inhaler can help if the cough causes wheezing — ask a pharmacist
long_term: Wash hands frequently — respiratory viruses spread mainly through hand contact
Avoid smoking — smokers get worse and longer-lasting bronchitis
Good nutrition and sleep maintain strong immunity against recurrent infections

see_doctor_if: Cough lasting more than 3 weeks without improvement
Coughing up blood or blood-streaked sputum
Difficulty breathing or chest tightness
High fever (above 38.5°C) that does not improve
Drenching night sweats or unexplained weight loss (possible TB)
Wheezing that does not improve with rest
home_remedies: Ginger and honey tea — anti-inflammatory, soothes airways, reduces cough
Steam with eucalyptus or Vicks — opens airways and loosens mucus
Thyme tea — traditional remedy with good evidence for bronchitis cough
Warm salt water gargle — soothes throat irritation
acute_bronchitis.local_context: Cough is one of the most common reasons Ugandans seek medical care. Most acute coughs are viral — the biggest mistake is taking antibiotics unnecessarily, which creates drug resistance without helping the illness. If a cough persists beyond 3 weeks and is associated with weight loss or night sweats, TB must be ruled out — GeneXpert sputum test is free at district hospitals.

fu_mdd_anhedonia.question: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy — hobbies, friends, food, or activities?

fu_mdd_function.question: Is this affecting your daily life — work, school, relationships, or basic self-care?

fu_mdd_safety.question: Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or that life is not worth living?

fu_lake_exposure.question: Have you been swimming in, wading through, or had contact with lake, river, or pond water recently — especially Lake Victoria or other freshwater bodies?

fu_abdominal_swelling.question: Is your abdomen (belly) noticeably swollen or enlarged — more than usual?

fu_sickle_cell_status.question: Have you been diagnosed with sickle cell disease — either SS (full sickle cell) or SC type?

fu_pain_location.question: Where is the pain mainly located — in your bones, joints, chest, abdomen, or all over?

fu_fever_scd.question: Do you have fever alongside this pain — temperature above 38°C or feeling very hot?

fu_pregnancy_weeks.question: How many weeks pregnant are you?

fu_blood_pressure_reading.question: Have you had your blood pressure measured recently? If so, what was the reading?

fu_headache_type.question: Is the headache severe — described as the worst headache you've ever had, or like a thunderclap?

fu_visual_changes.question: Are you experiencing any changes in your vision — blurring, seeing spots, or partial vision loss?

fu_delivery_date.question: When did you give birth — how many weeks or months ago?

fu_mood_duration.question: How long have you been feeling this low or sad since giving birth?

fu_bonding.question: Are you finding it difficult to bond with or feel warmth toward your baby — feeling distant or disconnected?

fu_thoughts_of_harm.question: Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or your baby? (This is asked in confidence to help keep you safe.)

fu_muac.question: If you have a measuring tape — measure the child's mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC). What does it measure?

fu_oedema.question: Does the child have swelling in both feet — if you press the top of the foot does a dent remain?

fu_feeding_history.question: Has the child been eating and drinking significantly less than normal over the past weeks?

fu_stool_character.question: How would you describe the diarrhoea — watery, loose, or greasy/oily and pale, with a very foul smell?

fu_duration.question: How long has this been going on?

fu_animal_contact.question: Have you been in close contact with livestock — cows, goats, sheep, or pigs — or handled raw meat or unpasteurised milk?

fu_raw_milk.question: Did you drink unpasteurised (raw/fresh) milk or eat fresh uncooked animal products recently?

fu_fever_level.question: How high is the fever — have you measured it? Is the child extremely hot?

fu_previous_seizures.question: Has this child had seizures before — and have they been diagnosed with febrile convulsions or epilepsy?

emergency_flags.name: Possible Brain Bleed / Meningitis
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ IMPORTANT: A sudden, severe headache described as the worst of your life — especially with a stiff neck — can be a sign of a serious brain condition. Please go to a hospital emergency department now. Do not wait.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Heart Attack
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: Chest pain with arm pain and sweating could be a heart attack. Call for help immediately or get to the nearest hospital as fast as possible. Do not drive yourself.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Stroke
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: Sudden weakness, confusion, or difficulty speaking could be a stroke. Every minute matters. Go to hospital immediately or call for emergency help.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Severe Malaria
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: High fever with confusion in Uganda must be treated as possible severe malaria. This is a medical emergency. Go to hospital immediately.

emergency_flags.name: Respiratory Emergency
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: Severe difficulty breathing requires immediate emergency care. Go to hospital now or call for help.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Appendicitis
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: Lower right abdominal pain with fever can be appendicitis — a surgical emergency. Go to hospital now. Do not eat or drink anything.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Meningococcal Disease
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: A non-blanching rash with fever and stiff neck could be meningococcal disease — one of the fastest-killing infections. Go to hospital immediately.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Heat Stroke
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: Confusion in extreme heat without sweating is heat stroke. Move to shade immediately, cool the body with water, and get to hospital urgently.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Stroke
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: These symptoms suggest a stroke. Every minute matters. Go to hospital immediately — do not wait to see if it gets better.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Cholera
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: Profuse watery diarrhoea can cause fatal dehydration within hours. Start ORS immediately and go to hospital today.

emergency_flags.name: Cerebral Malaria
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: Fever with confusion or seizures in Uganda means possible cerebral malaria or meningitis — both are life-threatening. Go to hospital immediately. Do not wait.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Peritonsillar Abscess
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: Severe sore throat with inability to open the mouth fully or drooling may be a peritonsillar abscess. Go to hospital today — it needs drainage.

emergency_flags.name: Status Epilepticus
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is a medical emergency. Call for help immediately and get to hospital now.
